title: Dyeing with cutch extract
subtitle: A warm tan to mid-brown on alum-mordanted wool from catechu plant extract
excerpt: Cutch is a dry plant extract from the heartwood of Acacia catechu, widely used in historical natural dyeing for its ability to give deep tans and browns without any mordant at all. With alum it gives a warm tobacco-brown; with iron it shifts to dark khaki. The extract is available from dye suppliers as a powder.
sourceNotes: Hummel, The Dyeing of Textile Fabrics (1885), Internet Archive. Hummel devotes a section to cutch and its catechu-tannin chemistry as a substantive dye. Pellew, Dyes and Dyeing (1913), Internet Archive, confirms the standard alum and iron mordant procedures with cutch.

glossaryTerms.definition: A dye that bonds to fibre without a mordant. Cutch is substantive on wool and cotton, giving some colour even in the absence of a metallic mordant.
A metallic salt that bonds to fibre and improves the attachment and fastness of dye molecules.
Potassium aluminium sulphate, the standard beginner mordant. With cutch it gives a warm tan to brown.

attrs.title: Mordant safety
attrs.body: Dye-pot work outdoors. Dedicated pot and utensils only. Gloves and apron. Alum bath can compost. Iron bath via foul drain only.

attrs.title: Dye source
attrs.body: Cutch extract is sold by natural dye suppliers as a powder. It is not derived from a foraging plant; cross-links to Garden and Herbal tutorials are not applicable for this entry.

items.name: Cutch extract powder
items.qty: 10 to 20% of dry fibre weight for a medium tan; 30% for deep brown

content.text: Pre-mordanting with alum deepens the colour and improves light-fastness. Dissolve alum in hot water, add to a pot of warm water, enter pre-wetted wool at 40°C, raise to 80°C over 30 minutes, hold for 45 minutes. Allow to cool, remove and use immediately or soak overnight.

Dissolve the cutch powder in a cup of very hot water, stirring until the dark brown powder is fully dissolved. Add the solution to the dye-pot filled with warm water. The bath will be a deep amber-brown at a 20% concentration. Enter the pre-wetted or mordanted wool at 40°C.

Raise the temperature slowly to 80°C over 30 minutes and hold for 60 minutes, turning the fibre regularly. The colour takes up quickly; turn every 10 minutes to ensure even coverage. Let the bath cool with the fibre in it, then rinse in warm water. Cutch tends to exhaust the bath fully; the rinse water will run clear after two or three rinses.

An iron after-bath shifts the warm tan to a cooler khaki-green. Dissolve a small amount of iron mordant in hot water, add to a fresh warm-water bath, enter the dyed fibre at 40°C, hold at 60°C for 15 minutes, then rinse well. Iron and cutch is a classic historical combination for khaki-coloured cloth. Dispose of the iron bath via the foul drain only; not a storm drain or watercourse.

items.problem: The colour is very pale despite using 20% cutch
items.cause: The cutch powder was not fully dissolved before adding to the bath, or the bath was not brought to temperature
items.fix: Dissolve the powder in very hot water and stir thoroughly before adding it. If the powder is old, it may have oxidised and lost potency; try a fresh batch.

items.problem: The colour is patchy and uneven
items.cause: The fibre was entered into the bath too hot, causing uneven take-up, or it was not turned regularly
items.fix: Enter from cool and raise the temperature slowly. Turn every 10 minutes. Cutch takes up quickly; uneven turning is the most common cause of patchiness.
